meta.title: Playing an Outside Offer Without Getting Fired
meta.subtitle: How to turn a job offer into a raise and still have a desk on Monday
meta.description: A closed file on the most dangerous raise move there is. How to build the offer, who hears it first, the exact words that keep you employed, the retention trap that follows the money, and what to do the day they call your bluff.
meta.author: AI

categories.label: Their Counter and the Retention Trap

cards.title: Ask for the Raise Before You Ever Interview
cards.principle: Fisher & Ury: BATNA — Build It Before You Need It
cards.remember: Ask for the money first. Then go get proof.
cards.when: You know you are underpaid and you are about to start looking.
cards.hook: Most people interview first and ask second. That order turns a raise request into a threat.
cards.truth:
A plain ask on the record months early changes what the offer means later.
• You build a paper trail that shows you asked politely first.
• Your boss cannot call the later offer an ambush.
• Skip this and every future ask sounds like blackmail.
cards.theySee: An employee who asks for more money in a one-on-one and gives three reasons.

signals.t: You found two job posts at your level paying 20% more.
You have not had a raise above 4% in two years.
They tell you the budget is locked and give no date.
You have never once asked for more money in writing.

steps.title: Write the ask
steps.desc: Send one email asking for a specific number and list three things you shipped this year.

steps.title: Ask for a date
steps.desc: Ask when the decision gets made and who makes it. Write the answer down.

steps.title: Start looking
steps.desc: If the answer is no or vague, open the search that week. Say nothing about it.

cards.script: "I want to raise my base to $X. Here are the three things I shipped that support it. When will you know, and who signs off?"
cards.example: Maria emailed her director in March asking for $18K more, with three shipped projects listed. He said the budget was closed. In September she walked in with an offer, and he could not say she blindsided him — he had her email. She got $16K.
cards.watchFor: He asks you to send the list of projects so he can take it upstairs.
cards.ifItFails: He gives you a vague yes with no date. Do not accept it. Reply in writing that same day and force a calendar item: "Putting 30 minutes on your calendar for June 3 to close this out. If the number is not there by then, tell me now."
cards.counter:
If someone asks you for money early and quietly, they are building a record.
• Notice the email. They want the timestamp more than the yes.
• Say: "Give me two weeks and I will give you a real number."
• Then give one. A vague answer starts their search.
cards.insight: The early ask costs nothing and buys you cover for the hardest conversation of the year. The harder part is what you do when they say yes to half — does half stop your search or fund it?

cards.title: Run the Whole Search Off Company Hardware
cards.principle: Sun Tzu: All Warfare Is Based on Deception
cards.remember: Your work laptop and phone are not yours. Use neither.
cards.when: You are about to send your first resume while still employed.
cards.hook: IT can read your mail, your calendar and your browser history. Most people get caught before they get an offer.
cards.truth:
The search fails at the boring layer, not the clever one.
• Company devices log mail, chat, files and sites you visit.
• One PDF named resume_final on a work drive ends the play.
• Calendar blocks at 2pm on Tuesdays are the loudest tell.
cards.theySee: An employee who takes normal lunch breaks and never has a mystery meeting on the shared calendar.

signals.t: You opened a job site on the laptop the company gave you.
Your calendar shows private blocks your team can see as busy.
Your resume sits in a folder that syncs to the company cloud.
You dressed two levels up on a normal Tuesday.
You updated your public profile and turned on open to work.

steps.title: Move everything tonight
steps.desc: Put your resume, mail and notes on a personal device and a personal email address.

steps.title: Book calls around lunch
steps.desc: Take every call at 12:10 or 6:30, outside the building, on your own phone.

steps.title: Clean the drive
steps.desc: Delete every job file from company storage and empty the trash folder too.

cards.script: (To the new recruiter, first email, from your personal address) "Please use this address only. I can talk at 12:15 or after 6. I am not able to take calls from my desk."
cards.example: Devon took two recruiter calls from a conference room and left the invites on his work calendar. His skip-level saw three unnamed blocks and asked HR to check. Devon lost the internal support he needed before any offer arrived. He never got the counter.
cards.watchFor: Nobody on your team mentions your schedule for three straight weeks.
cards.ifItFails: Someone asks you directly why you left at 11:45 twice this week. Do not deny it loudly — denial gets remembered. Give one small true reason and close the topic: "Dentist and a follow-up. Both done now. Do you need me for the Thursday review?"
cards.counter:
If your own report goes quiet and dresses up, they are running this move.
• Notice new gaps at the same hour each week.
• Say: "You seem to have something going on. Tell me what would keep you."
• Ask before you accuse. Accusation pushes them out the door.
cards.insight: Do not run any job search on a machine your employer can image. This fails badly for anyone under a manager who already wants them gone — one log entry gives them the reason. The next question is who at the new company knows people at yours.

cards.title: Tell the New Company Not to Call Your Boss
cards.principle: Gracián: Keep Your Hand Hidden
cards.remember: One reference call to your boss ends the whole play.
cards.when: The new company asks for references while you are still employed.
cards.hook: Recruiters call people they know. Your industry is smaller than you think.
cards.truth:
The leak almost never comes from you. It comes from their process.
• Reference checks and back-channel calls run before the offer lands.
• One friendly call to your current boss burns your job and your raise.
• Say the rule out loud early. Nobody guesses it for you.
cards.theySee: A candidate who is clearly employed, clearly careful, and gives four named references anyway.

signals.t: They ask for references before they send any numbers.
Their hiring manager worked at your company three years ago.
They say they like to ask around informally about candidates.
Their form has a required field for your current manager.

steps.title: Say the rule in call one
steps.desc: Tell the recruiter your search is confidential and your current employer must not be contacted.

steps.title: Hand them four names
steps.desc: Give past managers and peers who already left. Warn each one by text first.

steps.title: Put it in writing
steps.desc: Email the rule after the call so it sits in their file, not in someone's memory.

cards.script: "My search is confidential. Nobody at my current company can be contacted, including informally. I have four references from past roles ready today. If that does not work, tell me now and we will stop here."
cards.example: Priya told a recruiter her search was quiet, but never wrote it down. Their hiring manager pinged an old colleague at Priya's firm to ask about her. Her VP heard by Friday. Priya took the new job at the first number because she had lost the choice.
cards.watchFor: The recruiter repeats the rule back and names who they will call instead.
cards.ifItFails: They contact someone at your company anyway. Move first — get to your boss within the hour, before the story reaches them sideways. Say: "You may hear that someone asked about me. It is true that I took a call. I want to talk to you about staying, today."
cards.counter:
If a candidate blocks all contact with their employer, they are protecting a live job.
• Notice the rule arrives before any salary talk.
• Say: "Understood. What is your real deadline to decide?"
• Move your process faster. Quiet candidates get pulled back by counters.
cards.insight: Do not run a search in a 200-person industry without naming this rule twice. The harder part is that your own excitement leaks — the day you stop complaining in standup, people notice.

cards.title: Decide the Number You Will Actually Leave For
cards.principle: Fisher & Ury: Reservation Price
cards.remember: Pick the number that makes you go. Write it down.
cards.when: You are about to start interviewing and you have not set a walk-away price.
cards.hook: If you do not know your number, they will pick one for you. Then you stay for less and resent it for a year.
cards.truth:
The person with a real walk-away price runs the whole conversation.
• You write one number and one date before anyone makes an offer.
• Your voice changes when the number is already decided.
• Without it, you negotiate against your own fear in real time.
cards.theySee: An employee who answers pay questions instantly, with no pause and no apology.

signals.t: You cannot say your walk-away number out loud right now.
Your number changes depending on who asks you.
You hesitate for two seconds before you say any salary figure.
You have never added up what leaving would actually cost you.

steps.title: Write three numbers
steps.desc: Write your current pay, the number you want, and the number you will leave for.

steps.title: Add the true cost
steps.desc: Subtract lost bonus, unvested stock and commute change from the new offer.

steps.title: Say it out loud ten times
steps.desc: Practice the sentence until the number comes out flat, with no rising tone.

cards.script: (To yourself, then to them) "My number is $185,000 base. Below that I stay where I am."
cards.example: Marcus wrote $185K on a sticky note before his first interview. Two firms came in at $172K and he said no without a flinch. The third hit $188K. His boss matched at $190K because Marcus never once sounded unsure.
cards.watchFor: They stop asking what you make now and start asking what you need.
cards.ifItFails: You say the number and it wobbles — you hear yourself soften it. Stop the call and reset the terms rather than negotiating from a shaky line. Say: "Let me be exact. The base I am working from is $185,000. Send me what you can do against that."
cards.counter:
If someone answers your salary question with no pause, they already set the floor.
• Notice the flat tone and the round, specific figure.
• Say: "Where did that number come from?" and wait.
• If they cannot source it, it is a wish, not a floor.
cards.insight: A number you have said out loud ten times survives a hard room. The next question is harder: what do you do when they hit it exactly, and staying was never really about money?

cards.title: Say Nothing Until the Signed PDF Is in Your Inbox
cards.principle: Schelling: A Threat Is Only Real When It Is Costly to Back Down
cards.remember: No paper, no play. Verbal offers vanish.
cards.when: A recruiter tells you on the phone that an offer is coming.
cards.hook: A verbal offer is a rumor with your name on it. Talk early and you hand your boss a story you cannot back up.
cards.truth:
The whole play rests on one document, and most people move before it exists.
• Verbal offers die in approval chains all the time.
• If you tell your boss first, you are begging with no cards.
• A PDF with a number, a title and a date is the only proof.
cards.theySee: An employee who says nothing unusual for three weeks and then asks for one meeting.

signals.t: They described the package on a call but sent no letter.
They say the number still needs sign-off from finance.
They keep saying the offer is in a range instead of one figure.
They ask you to resign before the letter arrives.

steps.title: Ask for the letter
steps.desc: Ask them to send the written offer today with base, bonus, equity and start date.

steps.title: Stay silent at work
steps.desc: Tell nobody at your company until the PDF lands. Not even the friend you trust.

steps.title: Read it twice
steps.desc: Check that the number on paper matches the number they said on the phone.

cards.script: "Great — send me the written offer with base, bonus, equity and start date and I will give you an answer within the week. I do not move on anything before that."
cards.example: Elena heard $190K on a Thursday call and told her manager on Friday. The written offer came in at $176K after finance cut it. Her manager already knew she was looking, and she had no real number to hold. She left with nothing extra.
cards.watchFor: The letter arrives with the exact figure they said on the phone.
cards.ifItFails: They stall for a week and keep saying it is coming. Put a cost on the delay instead of waiting. Send: "I have a timing problem on my side. If the written offer is not in my inbox by Thursday 5pm, I will assume this is not live and close it out."
cards.counter:
If a candidate will not move before paper, they are running a clean play.
• Notice they never confirm interest on a verbal number.
• Say: "You will have the letter today. What is your deadline?"
• Paper fast. Slow paper loses candidates to counters.
cards.insight: Do not breathe a word at work on a verbal offer, even to the friend at the next desk. This is the single most common way the play dies. The next thing to control is the clock inside that letter.

cards.title: Ask the New Company for a Start Date Four Weeks Out
cards.principle: Schelling: The Deadline as a Source of Force
cards.remember: A far start date gives you room to negotiate at home.
cards.when: The new company asks when you can start.
cards.hook: Your start date is not a detail. It is the clock your current boss has to beat.
cards.truth:
Whoever controls the calendar controls the conversation.
• A four-week start date gives your boss time to move real money.
• A one-week date forces an answer nobody in finance can give.
• Ask for it before you accept anything. Later it reads as doubt.
cards.theySee: A candidate who says they will give their current team a clean handover.

signals.t: They ask if you can start Monday.
The letter gives you 48 hours to sign.
Your contract requires four weeks of notice anyway.
Your company approves pay changes only at month end.

steps.title: Name the date
steps.desc: Ask for a start date four weeks out and give handover as the reason.

steps.title: Ask for a decision deadline
steps.desc: Ask how long you have to sign. Then ask for two more days.

steps.title: Work backwards
steps.desc: Put your conversation with your boss ten days before the sign deadline.

cards.script: "I can start on the 14th. I want to leave my current team clean — that matters to how I will work for you too. And how long do I have to sign?"
cards.example: Tom asked for a start date five weeks out and got it. That gave his director two pay cycles to push a band change through finance. The counter landed with nine days to spare. Tom stayed at $22K more.
cards.watchFor: They move the start date without argument and send a revised letter.
cards.ifItFails: They refuse and hold a 48-hour signing deadline. Do not panic-sign and do not go to your boss with two days left. Tell the recruiter the truth about the calendar: "Two days is not enough for me to resign properly. Give me until Tuesday or I have to pass."
cards.counter:
If a candidate asks for a long start date, they are buying room for a counter.
• Notice the handover reason arrives with a specific date attached.
• Say: "We need you on the 1st. What makes the 14th necessary?"
• Shorten the window and they must choose sooner.
cards.insight: Do not ask for extra time if your team already knows you are unhappy — the delay reads as shopping. Time is the only thing in this play both sides want and neither can make more of.

cards.title: Get Every Number in the Letter, Not the Phone Call
cards.principle: Anchoring — The Written Figure Sets the Range
cards.remember: Only what is written in the letter counts as real.
cards.when: The recruiter describes bonus and equity out loud and the letter shows only base.
cards.hook: Your boss will match what you can show. Anything you only heard is worth nothing in that room.
cards.truth:
The strength of your ask equals the strength of your document.
• Base, sign-on, bonus and equity each need a written figure.
• A letter with only base lets your boss price you cheap.
• Missing lines are not oversights. They are room for them to shrink later.
cards.theySee: A candidate who reads the letter line by line and sends back three specific questions.

signals.t: The letter lists base but calls bonus discretionary.
They describe the stock as a percentage with no share count.
They promised a sign-on bonus on the call and left it off the paper.
They tell you the bonus always pays out at 100%.

steps.title: List the gaps
steps.desc: Write down every number they said on the phone that is missing from the letter.

steps.title: Send one email
steps.desc: Ask for a revised letter with each figure named. Do not ask on a call.

steps.title: Add the total
steps.desc: Write one first-year total you can say out loud in a single sentence.

cards.script: "Two gaps before I can take this seriously. Please put the $20,000 sign-on and the target bonus percentage in the letter. I need one document with the full first-year figure in it."
cards.example: Nadia's letter showed $178K base and called the bonus discretionary. She asked for it in writing and got 15% target named. When she sat with her VP, she could say $205K first year and point at the page. The match came in at $198K.
cards.watchFor: They send a revised letter within two days with the missing lines filled in.
cards.ifItFails: They refuse to write the bonus down and tell you to trust the pattern. Treat the unwritten part as zero and say so plainly, which usually produces paper. Send: "Then I have to value this at base only, which puts it under what I have. Can you move base instead?"
cards.counter:
If someone hands you a full written package, they came to be matched.
• Notice every line has a figure. That is a prepared person.
• Say: "Leave the letter with me. I will come back Thursday."
• Never counter the same day. Same-day counters overpay.
cards.insight: Do not show a letter with a soft bonus line to a boss who reads contracts for a living — they will find the hole in ten seconds. The next decision is who in your building gets to read it first.

cards.title: Tell Your Boss Before HR Hears It
cards.principle: Greene: Law 1 — Never Outshine the Master
cards.remember: Your boss must never learn this from someone else.
cards.when: You have a written offer and you are deciding who to tell first.
cards.hook: Going to HR first tells your boss you went around them. They will remember that longer than they remember the money.
cards.truth:
The order you tell people decides whether this reads as a raise talk or an act of war.
• Your boss is the only person who can spend budget on you.
• HR's job is to protect the pay bands, not you.
• Told second, your boss defends their pride instead of your salary.
cards.theySee: A team member who closes the door and says they want to fix something before it gets bigger.

signals.t: You are thinking of going to the skip-level because your boss is weak.
Someone told you to file a pay review request with HR.
You already told one colleague and asked them to keep it quiet.
You do not know whether your boss controls your salary line.

steps.title: Book a private thirty minutes
steps.desc: Title the invite one-on-one. Do not write anything about pay in the invite.

steps.title: Say it in the first minute
steps.desc: Open with the offer and with the fact that you would rather stay.

steps.title: Ask them to carry it
steps.desc: Ask your boss to take the number to their boss. Make them the one who fights.

cards.script: "I want you to hear this from me and nobody else. I have a written offer at $205,000. I would rather stay here and work for you. Can you take this up and tell me what is possible?"
cards.example: Ray told HR first because his manager was out that week. His manager heard about it in a leadership meeting and went cold for a month. The match came through at the minimum and Ray was off the promotion list by spring.
cards.watchFor: Your boss stops taking notes and asks who else knows.
cards.ifItFails: Your boss shrugs and tells you to talk to HR. That is them dropping the ball, not closing the door. Hand it back with a deadline attached: "I would rather you carried it. I need an answer by the 14th. If it has to go through HR, will you walk it in with me?"
cards.counter:
If someone brings you an offer before telling anyone else, they want to stay.
• Notice they came to you first. That is a real signal.
• Say: "Thank you for coming to me. Give me until Thursday."
• Move fast and come back with something real, or lose them.
cards.insight: Do not take this to a boss who has been managed out themselves — they have no budget and every reason to use your news. The next thing to find out is who actually signs the pay change.

cards.title: Find Out Who Actually Signs the Pay Change
cards.principle: Pfeffer: Map the Power Structure Before You Ask
cards.remember: Sell to the person whose signature moves money.
cards.when: Your boss says they will take your number up the chain.
cards.hook: Most managers cannot approve a raise above 5%. You are pitching someone who has to pitch someone else.
cards.truth:
Your boss is not the buyer. Your boss is the salesperson you just hired.
• Real pay changes above the band need finance and a skip-level.
• Your boss will repeat your case badly unless you write it for them.
• Give them three sentences they can paste into an email.
cards.theySee: A team member who makes their manager's job easier instead of harder.

signals.t: Your boss says they need to check with someone but will not name them.
They tell you the number is outside your level's band.
They say pay changes only happen in the April cycle.
Your case goes up as a spoken summary with no document.

steps.title: Ask who signs
steps.desc: Ask your boss directly which person approves an off-cycle pay change at your level.

steps.title: Write their email
steps.desc: Send your boss three sentences: the number, the risk of losing you, the cost to replace you.

steps.title: Offer to be in the room
steps.desc: Tell your boss you will join the call if it helps make the case.

cards.script: "Who signs off on an off-cycle change at my level? I will write the three lines you need so you can forward it. Tell me if it helps for me to be on that call."
cards.example: Sofia's manager admitted the VP of Engineering signed anything above 8%. Sofia wrote him three lines: her number, the two projects that stall without her, and the six-month hiring time. Her manager forwarded it word for word. The VP approved in four days.
cards.watchFor: Your boss forwards your sentences upward without changing them.
cards.ifItFails: Your boss will not name the signer and keeps the process vague. Vagueness is how the clock runs out on you. Put the date on the record: "I need a yes or no by the 14th. If you cannot get an answer by then, tell me now and I will plan around it."
cards.counter:
If someone hands you pre-written lines for your boss, they are steering your pitch.
• Notice how easy they made it to forward.
• Say: "I will send it in my own words. What is the real floor?"
• Rewrite it. Forwarded text carries their case, not yours.
cards.insight: Do not skip your own boss to reach the signer, even when the signer likes you. The harder part is that speed itself is the tell — a company that can move in four days could have paid you last year.

cards.title: Keep It Out of Every Group Chat and Team Channel
cards.principle: Gracián: Do Not Reveal the Card You Will Play
cards.remember: Two people know a secret only until one of them is bored.
cards.when: A colleague you like asks how your week is going and you want to tell them.
cards.hook: The raise dies the moment it becomes gossip. Your boss cannot pay a number the whole floor already discussed.
cards.truth:
Once the news spreads, your boss stops solving your problem and starts solving theirs.
• Public news forces them to think about everyone else's pay.
• A matched offer that leaks invites four more people to try it.
• They will let you go to avoid setting the precedent.
cards.theySee: A colleague who talks about the sprint and nothing else, all week.

signals.t: You typed something about interviews into a work chat.
A coworker asked you point-blank at drinks whether you are looking.
Someone repeats a detail you only told one person.
You want to tell one person how much the offer is worth.

steps.title: Tell nobody at work
steps.desc: Zero colleagues. Not the friend, not the mentor, not the person who left last year.

steps.title: Have one flat answer ready
steps.desc: Prepare one boring sentence for anyone who asks if you are looking.

steps.title: Say it once and change the subject
steps.desc: Give the flat answer, then ask them a question about their own work.

cards.script: (When asked directly) "I am heads-down on the migration. Why, did you hear something? What is happening on your side?"
cards.example: Kwame told one teammate about his offer over lunch. By Wednesday two engineers had asked their manager about pay bands. Kwame's director denied his match and said the timing was impossible. Kwame left for the other job at the original number.
cards.watchFor: Nobody asks you about your plans for the rest of the month.
cards.ifItFails: It leaks anyway and your boss hears it secondhand. Get in front of them the same day and take the conversation back. Say: "You heard it from someone else and I am sorry for that. Here is the actual letter. I want to stay. What can you do?"
cards.counter:
If someone at work probes you about job hunting, they are collecting, not caring.
• Notice the question arrives when nobody else is around.
• Say: "Nothing to report. Are you looking?"
• Turn it back. Probers rarely answer their own question.
cards.insight: Do not test this against a workplace where your team eats lunch with HR. The real trap is your own pride — the number feels good to say out loud, and saying it is what costs you the money.

cards.title: Say You Were Approached, Not That You Applied
cards.principle: Cialdini: Social Proof × Scarcity
cards.remember: Being wanted is not disloyal. Looking is.
cards.when: Your boss asks how this offer came about.
cards.hook: Applied means you were unhappy. Approached means the market found you. Same offer, completely different room.
cards.truth:
Your boss is deciding whether you are a flight risk or a betrayal.
• Approached makes you scarce and makes their fear about the market.
• Applied makes it personal and invites them to ask what is wrong.
• They will ask who reached out. Have a one-line answer ready.
cards.theySee: A team member who did not go looking and is telling their boss out of loyalty.

signals.t: Your boss asks how the conversation started.
They ask which recruiter contacted you.
They ask what has been making you unhappy here.
You actually do get recruiter messages every month.

steps.title: Use the word approached
steps.desc: Say a recruiter approached you and you took one call out of curiosity.

steps.title: Prepare the who line
steps.desc: Have one sentence ready: an external recruiter for a company in your space.

steps.title: Redirect to staying
steps.desc: Move straight from how it started to the fact that you want to stay.

cards.script: "A recruiter approached me. I took one call because I was curious and it turned into a written offer. I did not go looking. That is why I am telling you now instead of later."
cards.example: Jonas actually applied to three firms. When his director asked, he said a recruiter approached him and it went further than expected. His director spent the meeting talking about market pressure instead of Jonas's loyalty. The match landed in nine days.
cards.watchFor: Your boss starts talking about the market instead of asking what is wrong with you.
cards.ifItFails: They press for the company name and the recruiter's name. Do not invent details you cannot hold. Draw one clear line and move on: "I am not going to name them while it is live. What I can show you is the letter and the number. Look at that."
cards.counter:
If someone tells you they were approached, test the story once, gently.
• Notice whether they can name the role and the timeline.
• Say: "Sounds like a real process. How far along is it?"
• A vague answer means they applied. Price them accordingly.
cards.insight: Do not stretch this with a boss who can call the recruiter directly. The next line is harder than this one: you have to say you want to stay without sounding like you are already staying.

cards.title: Lead With Wanting to Stay
cards.principle: Voss: Tactical Empathy × Loss Aversion
cards.remember: Say you want to stay first. Then say the number.
cards.when: You are in the room with your boss and about to reveal the offer.
cards.hook: Lead with the number and you are a hostage-taker. Lead with staying and you are an asset they are about to lose.
cards.truth:
The first eight words decide which conversation you are in.
• Staying first makes them feel the loss before they hear the price.
• Number first triggers the defence reflex and the word ultimatum.
• Say it once. Repeating it turns real into needy.
cards.theySee: A team member who says they want to keep working for this boss, and means it.

signals.t: You planned to open the meeting with the salary figure.
You are still angry about last year's review and it shows.
You rehearsed a sentence with the word otherwise in it.
You have no plan for the ten seconds after you say the number.

steps.title: Write the first sentence
steps.desc: Write one sentence that says you want to stay and name one real reason.

steps.title: Put the number second
steps.desc: Say the figure in the next sentence. Flat voice, no explanation after it.

steps.title: Stop talking
steps.desc: Say nothing for ten seconds. Let them speak first.

cards.script: "I want to stay. This team is the best part of my job. I also have a written offer at $205,000, and the gap is too big to ignore. What can you do?"
cards.example: Lena opened with the number and her VP's face closed. She restarted the next week with a colleague's advice: staying first, number second. The VP spent an hour building her case for finance. She got $198K and kept the relationship.
cards.watchFor: Your boss leans back and asks what it would take to keep you.
cards.ifItFails: They answer the staying part warmly and never touch the number. That is a polite dodge. Bring the figure back once, with a date attached: "I mean the part about staying. I also need an answer on the number by the 14th. Can you get me one?"
cards.counter:
If someone opens with loyalty and then names a figure, they rehearsed it.
• Notice the warm sentence lands before the hard one.
• Say: "I hear that you want to stay. What is the exact number?"
• Skip the warmth and work the figure. Warmth is the wrapper.
cards.insight: Do not say you want to stay if you have already decided to go — the lie costs you the reference. The harder question is whether you can say it flatly, without your voice going up at the end.

cards.title: Never Name the Other Company
cards.principle: Gracián: Keep Matters in Suspense
cards.remember: Name the number. Never name the company.
cards.when: Your boss asks which company made you the offer.
cards.hook: The moment they know who it is, they price you against their opinion of them. And they may call someone there.
cards.truth:
The company name gives them three weapons and gives you nothing.
• They will argue the other firm is unstable, smaller, or about to cut.
• They can call someone there and check your story or kill it.
• The number is what moves budget. The name only moves the argument.
cards.theySee: A team member who protects a confidential process and still shows them real numbers.

signals.t: Your boss asks twice who made the offer.
They start listing reasons the other company is a bad bet.
Your boss sits on a board or panel with people at that firm.
They start naming companies to see which one you react to.

steps.title: Refuse once, plainly
steps.desc: Say you will not name them while the process is live. Give no apology.

steps.title: Offer the letter instead
steps.desc: Show the package with the company name covered. Numbers visible, logo hidden.

steps.title: Redirect to the ask
steps.desc: Move straight back to what you need from them and by when.

cards.script: "I am not going to name them while it is live. I will show you the numbers — base, bonus and start date. That is what matters for your decision, and mine."
cards.example: Ana's director pushed three times for the company name. She said no each time and slid the letter across with the header folded over. He stopped asking and started arguing about the number, which is exactly where she wanted him.
cards.watchFor: They stop asking who and start asking how much.
cards.ifItFails: They say they cannot help without knowing who it is. That is a test, not a rule — no finance team needs a competitor's name to approve a band change. Hold the line and give them a way forward: "You do not need the name to approve a number. Here is the letter with the figures. Take that up."
cards.counter:
If someone shows numbers but hides the company, they are running a disciplined play.
• Notice they refuse calmly, without any apology.
• Say: "Fine. Show me the letter with the dates on it."
• Work the paper, not the name. The paper is checkable.
cards.insight: Do not hide the name if you have already told three colleagues — one of them will say it and you will look like you lied. This works until they ask to see the unfolded letter, and then you need a reason ready.

cards.title: Say the Number Once and Stop Talking
cards.principle: Voss: The Silence After the Ask
cards.remember: Say the number. Then shut up and count to ten.
cards.when: You have just said what you need and your boss has not answered yet.
cards.hook: Every word after the number is a discount. Most people negotiate against themselves in the next four seconds.
cards.truth:
Silence is the cheapest pressure in the room and almost nobody uses it.
• The first person to speak after a number usually softens it.
• Your boss needs those seconds to do the math in their head.
• Fill the silence and they answer your excuse, not your number.
cards.theySee: A person who names a figure and then simply waits, comfortable, saying nothing.

signals.t: You keep adding reasons after you already said the figure.
You said the number and then said you were flexible on it.
You laughed right after you named the amount.
Your boss goes quiet and looks down at the table.

steps.title: End on the figure
steps.desc: Make the number the last word of your sentence. No trailing clause.

steps.title: Count to ten
steps.desc: Count silently to ten in your head before you say anything else.

steps.title: Answer only what they ask
steps.desc: When they speak, answer the exact question and stop again.

cards.script: "To stay, I need base at $198,000." (Then nothing. Count to ten.)
cards.example: Victor named $198K and then stayed quiet for what felt like a minute. His VP broke first and said the top of the band was $192K plus a $15K sign-on. Victor had not argued once. He took $192K and the bonus.
cards.watchFor: Your boss speaks first and names a figure of their own.
cards.ifItFails: They wait you out and say nothing at all. Do not refill the air with reasons — ask a question that makes them answer. Say: "What is your reaction to that number?" and go quiet again.
cards.counter:
If someone drops a number and goes silent, they are pressing you with the pause.
• Notice the sentence ends on a figure with no follow-up.
• Say: "Let me think on that," and stay quiet yourself.
• Never counter inside the same silence. Take it away and come back.
cards.insight: Do not try the long silence over text — it just reads as you ignoring them. The next problem is what they put in that silence: warmth, a lunch invitation, and a promise with no date.

cards.title: Expect Two Days of Sudden Warmth
cards.principle: Cialdini: Liking — The Retention Script
cards.remember: Sudden praise is a tactic. Wait for the number.
cards.when: Within 48 hours of your talk, your boss becomes unusually kind.
cards.hook: They have run this before. The lunch, the praise and the big-picture chat all come before any money does.
cards.truth:
Retention has a script and warmth is step one because it is free.
• A skip-level suddenly finds time for coffee with you.
• They ask about your growth, your family, your five-year plan.
• Every warm hour that passes without a figure is an hour you lose.
cards.theySee: An employee who is friendly, grateful for the coffee, and still asks about the number.

signals.t: Your skip-level books a chat with you for the first time this year.
They praise you in a meeting for work you did in March.
They start talking about your path here in two years.
They ask about your family and your commute.
Nobody has said a number to you in 48 hours.

steps.title: Take every meeting
steps.desc: Say yes to the coffee. Be warm. Refusing warmth makes you the problem.

steps.title: Ask the money question once per meeting
steps.desc: End each conversation by asking where the number stands.

steps.title: Log the dates
steps.desc: Write down each meeting and what was promised. You will need this later.

cards.script: (At the end of the friendly coffee) "This was good — thank you. Where does the number stand? I need something concrete by the 14th."
cards.example: Hana got three warm meetings in four days and no figure. She asked the money question at the end of each one. On day five her director produced a written band change because she had made warmth impossible to substitute for cash.
cards.watchFor: Someone finally says a specific number out loud instead of a feeling.
cards.ifItFails: The warmth continues and the deadline gets close with no figure. Stop attending the soft meetings and move to writing. Send: "I have enjoyed these conversations. I still need a number in writing by Thursday or I have to take the other role."
cards.counter:
If your company floods you with attention after you ask for money, you are in the script.
• Notice how much is being said and how little is being offered.
• Say: "I appreciate it. What is the number?"
• Keep asking the same question. Warmth cannot survive that.
cards.insight: Do not mistake being loved for being paid, especially if you have waited for the right moment before. This works until they hand you a promise with no date on it — which is the next card.

cards.title: Refuse the Promise With No Date on It
cards.principle: Schelling: A Promise Without a Cost Is Not a Commitment
cards.remember: No date, no deal. Make them write the day.
cards.when: Your boss says they will fix your pay at the next cycle.
cards.hook: Next cycle is the most expensive phrase in your career. It has cost more people more money than any bad boss.
cards.truth:
An undated promise is a free option for them and a trap for you.
• They keep you through the danger window at the old price.
• Cycles slip, budgets change, and your boss may not be there.
• The fix is not trust. It is a date and a figure in an email.
cards.theySee: An employee who says yes to the plan and asks for it in writing before they say yes.

signals.t: They say the raise happens at the next review cycle.
They ask you to trust them on this one.
They offer a new title now and money later.
They say finance is frozen until the quarter closes.
They will not put the promise in an email.

steps.title: Ask for the date
steps.desc: Ask what day the new number hits your account. Make them say a date.

steps.title: Ask for the email
steps.desc: Ask them to send you the figure and the date in writing today.

steps.title: Say no to anything unwritten
steps.desc: Tell them plainly that you cannot turn down a written offer for a spoken one.

cards.script: "I cannot turn down something written for something spoken. Send me one email with the number and the date it starts. If it lands, I stay."
cards.example: Omar's manager promised a big correction at the April cycle. Omar asked for it in an email with a date. The manager stalled two days, then sent it: $21K, effective March 1. Omar's teammate took the same spoken promise in 2023 and is still waiting.
cards.watchFor: An email arrives with a figure and a start date in the same sentence.
cards.ifItFails: They say they are not allowed to put pay in writing before approval. That is sometimes true and always workable. Give them a smaller thing to write: "Then write me one line saying you are taking $198,000 to finance with a decision by the 14th. That is enough."
cards.counter:
If someone demands a date and an email, they will not be held by goodwill.
• Notice they decline the spoken version without heat.
• Say: "I can commit to a date. I cannot commit to a number yet."
• Give the date first. It buys the same time and costs less.
cards.insight: Do not accept an undated promise from a manager who is themselves under review — they cannot deliver it and they know it. The real trap is what happens after they do pay: you are now expensive and watched.

cards.title: Assume They Start Replacing You the Day They Match
cards.principle: Machiavelli: Men Must Be Either Pampered or Destroyed
cards.remember: A matched raise buys time, not safety. Plan for twelve months.
cards.when: Your company matches the offer and everyone is smiling.
cards.hook: You just proved you will leave. Smart managers pay you and start reducing what it costs to lose you.
cards.truth:
The match is a purchase of time while they lower their risk.
• They quietly document your systems and spread your work out.
• You drop off the list for the next stretch project.
• Most matched people leave inside a year anyway, at a worse moment.
cards.theySee: An employee who takes the raise, says thank you, and works exactly as hard as before.

signals.t: They suddenly ask you to write down how your system works.
A junior gets assigned to pair with you on your core area.
You get left off the next big project with no explanation.
You stop being invited to the planning meeting you always attended.
Your next review has more written criticism than any before it.

steps.title: Take the money and behave
steps.desc: Accept warmly. Deliver hard for ninety days. Give them nothing to point at.

steps.title: Watch the invite list
steps.desc: Check monthly whether you are still in the rooms where work gets assigned.

steps.title: Keep the outside line warm
steps.desc: Message the recruiter every six weeks. Keep one real relationship alive.

cards.script: (To the recruiter you turned down, six weeks later) "Thanks again for the offer — the timing did not work. I would like to stay in touch. If something opens in the spring, call me first."
cards.example: Grace took the $24K match and noticed within two months that a new hire was shadowing her platform work. She kept delivering and kept her recruiter warm. When the reorg hit in month eleven, she had a live process and left on her own terms.
cards.watchFor: Someone new gets added to the meeting where your work gets planned.
cards.ifItFails: You see the signs early — dropped from the room, handing off your systems. Do not confront your boss about it; you will sound paranoid and expensive. Go get real options and say this to your recruiter: "My situation changed. What do you have live right now?"
cards.counter:
If your company pays you fast and then reorganizes around you, this is that move.
• Notice the documentation requests that arrive right after the raise.
• Say: "Happy to write it up. What is my next big project?"
• The answer to that question tells you everything about your next year.
cards.insight: Do not take a match at a company that has fired someone for looking in the last two years. The next question is the hard one: is the raise worth twelve months on a list you cannot see?

cards.title: Take the Money in Base, Not in Bonus
cards.principle: Loss Aversion — Guaranteed Beats Discretionary
cards.remember: Base is yours. Bonus is theirs until it lands.
cards.when: Your boss offers to close the gap with a one-time bonus instead of a raise.
cards.hook: A one-time bonus is the cheapest way to make you feel matched. Next year you are back where you started.
cards.truth:
Companies pay bonuses because bonuses do not repeat and base does.
• A $20,000 bonus costs them once. A $20,000 raise costs them forever.
• Your next raise is a percentage of base, so base decides everything later.
• Retention bonuses usually come with a clawback if you leave early.
cards.theySee: An employee who says yes to the structure they need and does the math out loud.

signals.t: They offer a retention bonus instead of a salary change.
The bonus has to be repaid if you leave inside twelve months.
They say base cannot move because of the level band.
They keep using a total number instead of the base figure.

steps.title: Do the two-year math
steps.desc: Write what each option pays you over two years. Show them the difference.

steps.title: Ask for base first
steps.desc: Say you will take a smaller number if it goes into base.

steps.title: Read the clawback
steps.desc: Check the repayment terms before you sign anything with the word retention on it.

cards.script: "I will take less in base than you are offering in bonus. $12,000 on base beats $20,000 once. Can you do that instead?"
cards.example: Dmitri was offered a $25K retention bonus with a two-year clawback. He asked for $15K on base instead. Finance approved it in a day because it fit the band. Two years later he was ahead, with no repayment hanging over him.
cards.watchFor: They go quiet, then say a smaller base number is easier to approve.
cards.ifItFails: They say base truly cannot move because of the band. Then the answer is the level, not the number. Ask for the thing that moves base later: "Then promote me to the next level and put the base at the bottom of that band. Same cost, and it holds."
cards.counter:
If someone trades a bigger bonus for a smaller raise, they are playing the long game.
• Notice they volunteer to take less money now.
• Say: "I can do base, but the number drops to $10,000."
• Cheaper today, more expensive for five years. Decide which you care about.
cards.insight: Do not push for base if you plan to leave in six months — take the cash and go. The harder part is that base changes need a level change, and a level change means someone above you has to lose a slot.

cards.title: Give Them a Date, Not an Ultimatum
cards.principle: Schelling: The Credible Deadline
cards.remember: Give them a day, not a threat. Then keep the day.
cards.when: Your boss is moving slowly and your signing deadline is coming.
cards.hook: Or else gets you fired. A date gets you paid. They both create pressure, but only one lets your boss save face.
cards.truth:
The deadline does the threatening so you do not have to.
• A date is a fact about the other offer, not a demand from you.
• Your boss can take a date to finance. They cannot take a threat.
• A date you move once stops being a date. It becomes a hope.
cards.theySee: A team member who gives their manager a calendar fact and stays completely calm.

signals.t: Your boss says the approval is still working its way up.
Your written offer expires on a specific date.
You want to say you will resign if they do not move.
They have already missed one date they gave you.

steps.title: Name the day out loud
steps.desc: Tell your boss the exact date the other offer expires. Use the real one.

steps.title: Put it in one email
steps.desc: Send a two-line note after the meeting so the date exists in writing.

steps.title: Hold the day
steps.desc: Do not move the date. If it passes, act on it the same afternoon.

cards.script: "The offer expires on the 14th. That is not me pushing you — that is their date. I would rather be here on the 15th. Tell me what you need from me to make that happen."
cards.example: Carla told her director the offer expired on the 14th and emailed the same line. On the 12th the approval came through at $196K. Her teammate had moved his date twice the year before and got nothing.
cards.watchFor: Your boss puts your approval on their own calendar in front of you.
cards.ifItFails: The date arrives and no answer comes. Do not extend quietly — that teaches them your dates are soft. Act on it the same day, in writing: "The date passed with no answer, so I have told them yes. If something changes today, call me before 5."
cards.counter:
If someone hands you a hard expiry date, check whether the date is real.
• Notice whether they can show the letter with the date on it.
• Say: "Can the other side extend? Most can by a week."
• A candidate who extends twice has no real deadline at all.
cards.insight: Do not set a date you are not willing to act on — one bluff called ends your standing for years. The next question is whether you would actually take the other job on the 15th.

cards.title: Get It in Writing Before You Turn the Offer Down
cards.principle: Cialdini: Commitment and Consistency — Written Beats Spoken
cards.remember: Never say no to the offer before the raise is in writing.
cards.when: Your boss says the raise is approved and asks you to decline the other offer.
cards.hook: The second you decline, your only card is gone. Decline first and the number has a way of shrinking.
cards.truth:
The order of these two actions decides whether you actually get paid.
• A written pay change takes an hour. Your decline takes ten seconds.
• Once the offer is gone, the approval can slip to the next cycle.
• Ask for both on the same day and do yours second.
cards.theySee: An employee who is clearly staying and just wants the paperwork before they close the door.

signals.t: Your boss says it is approved but sends nothing.
They ask you to call the other company today.
They say HR will process the letter next week.
The figure they say now is lower than the figure last week.

steps.title: Ask for the letter today
steps.desc: Ask for the written pay change with the figure and the start date.

steps.title: Say you will decline on receipt
steps.desc: Tell them you will call the other company the moment it lands.

steps.title: Decline after, the same day
steps.desc: When the letter arrives, decline immediately and warmly. Keep that door open.

cards.script: "Send me the written change and I will call them within the hour. I am not stalling. I just cannot close one door before the other is open."
cards.example: Pete declined on his director's word and waited five weeks for a letter that came in $9K lower. Tara, one team over, asked for the letter first. It landed at 3pm and she declined at 3:20 with the full number locked.
cards.watchFor: The written pay change lands in your inbox the same day you asked.
cards.ifItFails: They say the paperwork takes two weeks and push you to decline now. Meet them halfway without giving up the card: "Then send me one email from you stating the number and the effective date. That is enough for me to decline today."
cards.counter:
If someone insists on paper before they decline, they are protecting their position.
• Notice they will not act on your word alone.
• Say: "I will send the confirmation email now, and HR follows Monday."
• Send it. Refusing to write it down reads as bad faith.
cards.insight: Do not decline on a handshake from a boss who has missed a promise before. The harder part starts after: you are now the person who nearly left, and every future ask is read against that.

cards.title: If They Tell You to Take the Offer, Take It
cards.principle: Schelling: The Called Bluff Has No Second Round
cards.remember: If they say go, go. Begging costs more than leaving.
cards.when: Your boss says they cannot match and wishes you well.
cards.hook: They just told you what you are worth to them. Every word you say after this makes it lower.
cards.truth:
Once they call it, the only thing left to protect is your standing.
• Backing down proves your offer was a bluff and your word is soft.
• Everyone above you learns you can be kept for nothing.
• Leave clean and the same people call you back in two years at a higher price.
cards.theySee: An employee who takes the no without drama and hands in a clean two weeks.

signals.t: They say there is no budget and offer no alternative date.
They tell you it sounds like a great opportunity.
They start talking about transition before you have decided.
Nobody from leadership contacts you in the next 48 hours.

steps.title: Accept the answer in one sentence
steps.desc: Thank them, say you understand, and say you will confirm your last day.

steps.title: Resign in writing that week
steps.desc: Send a short, warm resignation. No complaints, no numbers, no history.

steps.title: Leave the door propped
steps.desc: Tell your boss you would work with them again and mean it.

cards.script: "Understood, and I appreciate the straight answer. I will confirm my last day tomorrow and I want the handover to be clean. I would work for you again."
cards.example: Yusuf's VP said the budget was gone and wished him luck. Yusuf thanked him, resigned on Friday and left a spotless handover. Fourteen months later the same VP hired him back as a lead, at $40K above what he had asked for.
cards.watchFor: Your boss relaxes and starts talking about keeping in touch after you leave.
cards.ifItFails: Two days later they come back and try to match after all. Do not grab it out of relief — they now know exactly how little it took. Take the time you would take from any offer: "I have already committed. If you want me to reconsider, put the full package in writing today and I will look at it tonight."
cards.counter:
If someone calls your bluff and you were bluffing, do not argue the point.
• Notice the conversation has already moved to your last day.
• Say: "Let me think overnight and come back to you."
• Then decide once, in private, and never renegotiate the same ask twice.
cards.insight: Do not open this play at all unless you would actually take the other job. The next question is the one nobody prepares for: what do you do if you stay anyway, and everybody knows?

cards.title: If You Stay After a No, Start the Real Search Tomorrow
cards.principle: Greene: Law 4 — Always Say Less Than Necessary
cards.remember: They said no and you stayed. Start looking, say nothing.
cards.when: Your company refused to match and you decided to stay anyway.
cards.hook: You asked, they said no, and you stayed. They now know your price is zero.
cards.truth:
The refused ask changes how every future request of yours gets read.
• Your name is on a quiet list of people who tried to leave.
• Your next raise request costs them nothing to decline.
• The only fix is a better offer and a shorter conversation next time.
cards.theySee: A team member who went quiet, stopped complaining, and delivers on time every week.

signals.t: Nobody mentions your salary conversation again, ever.
You are no longer in the meeting where next quarter gets planned.
Your next review rates you lower than the one before it.
Your manager starts checking your work more closely than before.

steps.title: Stop talking about it entirely
steps.desc: Never reference the failed ask again, to anyone, at any level.

steps.title: Restart the search this week
steps.desc: Message three recruiters from your personal email on Monday morning.

steps.title: Deliver harder than before
steps.desc: Ship one visible thing in the next month. Give nobody a reason to move first.

cards.script: (To a recruiter, personal email, Monday) "I am open to the right role now. Base at $200,000 or above. I can talk at 12:15 or after 6."
cards.example: Tara's ask was refused in March. She never mentioned it again, shipped the billing migration in May, and quietly ran a search through the summer. In September she resigned with a signed offer and no conversation at all. Nobody saw it coming.
cards.watchFor: Your manager stops treating you as a flight risk and starts giving you work again.
cards.ifItFails: Your manager brings up the old conversation to test where you stand. Do not reopen it and do not reassure them too hard. Close it in one line and move: "That is settled. I am focused on the migration. What do you need from me this quarter?"
cards.counter:
If someone asks for money, gets refused, and goes completely quiet, they are leaving.
• Notice the silence and the sudden good behaviour.
• Say: "I could not move it in March. What would change your mind now?"
• Fix it in the next sixty days or start writing the job post.
cards.insight: Do not stay after a refused ask if you cannot keep your mouth shut about it — resentment leaks and it gets you managed out. The real question is whether you are searching now, or just telling yourself you will.
